messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Walter is a sixty-seven-year-old widower who worked for decades as a military medic, a job that had trained him to stay calm under fire and to trust his hands no matter what. He lives alone in a small house on a quiet street, and for the past two years he has not driven a car and has avoided being a passenger in one as well. That began after the accident: a clear autumn afternoon, a four‑lane highway, a pickup truck that crossed the median and hit his sedan head‑on. Walter remembers the moment of impact but not the seconds before or after; what stays with him is the smell of burnt rubber and gasoline that filled the cabin, and the sound of metal tearing, a sound he can still hear in his head when the memory surfaces, as if it is playing through a speaker in a room he cannot leave. The other driver was later found to have a blood‑alcohol level three times the legal limit. Walter spent two weeks in the hospital with a fractured pelvis and a concussion.

In the months that followed, Walter found he could no longer sit in a car without his heart slamming against his ribs and his hands going slick with sweat. At first he thought it was just nerves, that he would get over it, but the physical reaction grew worse rather than better. He stopped accepting rides from his neighbor, stopped going to the grocery store except on foot, stopped visiting his son and daughter‑in‑law because they lived a twenty‑minute drive away. Being a passenger made him feel trapped, helpless, certain that another collision was only a moment away. He did not consciously decide to isolate himself; the choice felt like the only safe one.

What frightened him most, though, was something interior. In the quiet of his house, Walter began to watch his own thoughts. He would catch himself thinking about the crash and then panic, wondering if dwelling on it meant he was losing his mind. He started to try hard not to think about the event at all, but the effort itself became a kind of vigilance. He would notice a smell—once, the neighbor was grilling and the charred meat sent him straight back to the burnt odor in the wrecked car—and his body would react before his mind caught up: his stomach dropped, his jaw clenched, and he felt a surge of adrenaline that made no sense for a barbecue. He became jumpy at ordinary sounds: a truck backfiring down the street, a pan dropping in the kitchen, a door closing too sharply. Each time he startled, he told himself he was a coward, a weak person who could not handle what plenty of other people handled every day.

The memory itself felt strange to him. When he tried to describe the accident to his doctor, his words got tangled and he lost the thread halfway through, as though the story belonged to someone else and he was only a poor narrator. Sometimes he would sit and wonder if he had actually done something wrong, if he had acted too slowly or failed to see the truck in time, even though the police report had been clear: the other driver was drunk, there was nothing Walter could have done. But that knowledge did not shake the conviction that the event happened because of the way he behaved—that he had missed some signal, some duty of alertness that a good medic never misses. He came to believe he could not trust his own judgment anymore. If he had failed that day, how could he trust himself to do the right thing in anything else?

The weeks turned into a year, then two. His son called every Sunday and could hear the flatness in Walter’s voice, but Walter always said he was fine, just tired. He avoided talking about the accident because talking about it meant thinking about it, and thinking about it made him feel as though he was falling apart. He began to notice that his own mind felt like an enemy he had to police: he would check what he was thinking every few minutes, looking for signs of craziness—a memory popping up, a vivid sound, a flash of the crumpled hood. He told himself this was the only way to stay in control.

What finally brought Walter to seek help was not his own distress but something his son said over the phone last week. “Dad, you haven’t left the house in two months. You don’t even try. That’s not you.” Walter hung up and sat in the dark living room, and for the first time he acknowledged that maybe he could not fix this alone. He called a clinic the next morning. He still does not know exactly what he hopes for—maybe just to stop being afraid of his own thoughts, maybe to believe that he is not as weak as he feels. But he also fears that if he really opens the door to the memory, he will find out that he really is going crazy, that he will never drive again, that the crash will have taken everything it touched.

missing_explanations: The vignette does not describe any instance of Walter reacting to or being triggered by the smell of alcohol. It mentions the other driver had a high blood-alcohol level but no olfactory trigger related to alcohol smell.
